title: Can a curved figure have one, two or four fold lines?
description: Three figures with curved edges are drawn, one with exactly one matching fold, one with exactly two and one with exactly four. The same curve is placed on each matching side.
teaching_notes: One idea: a curved figure keeps a line of symmetry when the same curve is placed on both matching sides. Any correct drawing is fine. Watch for students who draw a circle, which has too many folds, or who add a curve to one side only.

source: Draw the following. In each case, the figure should contain at least one curved boundary. (a) A figure with exactly one line of symmetry. (b) A figure with exactly two lines of symmetry. (c) A figure with exactly four lines of symmetry.
video_script.why: The child builds curved figures with a chosen number of matching folds by copying the same curve on matching sides.
video_script.substitution: Start with a figure that has the folds we want, and make some edges curved, keeping the same curve on each matching side.
video_script.anchor: Three curved figures to draw, with exactly one, exactly two and exactly four matching folds
video_script.payoff_line: Put the same curve on each matching side.

final_answer.value: any correct drawing, for example a semicircle with one line, an oval with two lines, and a square with round bumps with 4 lines
final_answer.spoken: any correct drawing works, for example a semicircle with one line, an oval with two lines, and a square with round bumps with four lines

never_show: the example drawings before their steps
maths_rules: A line of symmetry is a fold line along which one half covers the other exactly.
A semicircle has exactly one line, the one that cuts the straight edge in half at a right angle.
An oval has exactly two lines, one along its long side and one along its short side.
A square with the same round bump on each of its four sides has exactly four lines.
A circle is not used, because it has more folds than we want.
video_script.design: One idea: the same curve on matching sides keeps the folds. Assumes the child knows the folds of a rectangle and a square. The three drawing boxes stay on the board from the hook to the end.
